body:
Meaning of a circular economy

Industries and cities depend on natural resources such as water, minerals, fuels and land. In a conventional linear economy, resources are extracted, converted into products, consumed and eventually discarded. This approach can increase the demand for fresh raw materials and create large quantities of waste.

A circular economy seeks to keep products, materials and other resources in productive use for as long as practical. It reduces unnecessary consumption, extends the useful life of products, recovers valuable materials and manages unavoidable waste safely.

Circular economy: An economic approach that reduces resource consumption and waste generation by preventing waste, reusing products and resources, recovering materials and maintaining their value within the economy.

A circular economy does not mean that every material can be recycled indefinitely. Some materials deteriorate during use, some become contaminated, and some recycling processes consume substantial energy. The objective is to reduce overall environmental pressure while maintaining useful economic activity.

Resource efficiency and circularity

Resource efficiency means obtaining more useful output from a given quantity of resources or producing the same output with fewer resources. A textile unit that reduces its water requirement per metre of fabric becomes more water-efficient.

Circularity goes further by keeping resources in use. If treated wastewater from a city replaces fresh water in a textile-processing unit, water that would otherwise be discharged becomes a useful industrial input.

ConceptMain concernIllustration
Resource efficiencyUsing fewer inputs for a useful outputReducing water consumption during textile processing
ReuseUsing a resource again without necessarily converting it into a new materialUsing suitably treated wastewater for industrial cooling
RecyclingProcessing discarded material into usable materialRecovering metal from industrial scrap
Cleaner productionPreventing pollution and waste at their sourceImproving a process so that less waste is generated
Safe disposalManaging unusable residues without unacceptable pollutionSending suitable hazardous residues to an authorised disposal facility

The waste-management hierarchy

Environmental management generally gives priority to actions that prevent waste rather than actions that merely dispose of it after generation.

  1. Prevention and reduction: Avoid unnecessary material use and reduce waste at the production stage.
  2. Reuse: Use a product, component or suitable resource again.
  3. Recycling: Recover materials for further productive use, including appropriate biological processing of organic waste.
  4. Recovery: Obtain useful energy or material value from suitable residual waste when higher-value options are not practical.
  5. Disposal: Safely manage remaining waste that cannot be appropriately recovered.

This hierarchy is a general decision principle. The actual choice must also consider pollution, resource use, safety, available technology and applicable law. Recycling a contaminated material in an unsafe manner is not preferable to its environmentally sound treatment.

Why Gujarat is important

Gujarat has major industrial concentrations in textiles, chemicals, petrochemicals, ceramics and engineering. It also has large urban centres and important coastal commercial activities. These features create opportunities for resource-efficient production but also increase the need for reliable water supplies, waste treatment and pollution prevention.

Water is especially important. Freshwater availability is uneven, and industrial, agricultural and urban users may compete for the same supplies. Reusing suitably treated wastewater can reduce pressure on freshwater resources. Shared industrial facilities can also make waste treatment and resource recovery more practical for groups of enterprises.

Environmental benefit depends on actual performance. A project should not be called sustainable merely because it recycles some waste. It must also control emissions, protect water and soil, handle residual waste and avoid excessive resource consumption elsewhere.

Prelims focus

  • A linear economy generally follows extraction, production, consumption and disposal.
  • A circular economy gives priority to keeping resources and materials in productive use.
  • Resource efficiency and circularity are related but are not identical concepts.
  • Waste prevention is preferred to recycling, recovery and disposal in the waste hierarchy.
  • Trap: Circular economy does not mean that all waste is recyclable or that pollution-control requirements disappear.

[Sources: National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT), Class 11, Indian Economic Development, chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 164–172; NCERT, Class 8, Resources and Development, chapter 5, Industries, printed pp. 50–53; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, rule 3, definition of waste hierarchy, notification dated 27 January 2026, consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Understanding the Circular Economy and Resource Efficiency in Gujarat

body:
How industrial clusters develop

An industrial cluster is a geographical concentration of industries and associated economic activities. Factories may locate close to one another because they can obtain raw materials, transport, electricity, water, labour, markets and supporting services more conveniently.

Industries located near one another may also benefit from shared roads, pipelines, warehouses, treatment facilities and specialised service providers. These advantages can reduce costs and improve production efficiency.

However, concentration also creates environmental challenges. Several industries drawing water from the same area or releasing effluents into a common drainage system can place considerable pressure on local resources. Therefore, industrial planning must consider environmental infrastructure alongside production infrastructure.

Major industrial concentrations in Gujarat

Gujarat's industrial geography offers several examples of activities that could benefit from resource sharing. The opportunities in the following table are possible applications, not claims that every listed project has already been implemented.

Industrial areaImportant activitiesResource-efficiency opportunity
Ahmedabad and VadodaraTextiles, engineering, chemicals and related manufacturingWater conservation, material recovery and shared effluent management
Surat, Pandesara and SachinTextiles and other manufacturing activitiesTreated wastewater reuse and shared treatment facilities
Ankleshwar, Panoli and NandesariChemical and related industriesCommon effluent treatment and controlled recovery of suitable materials
Vapi and SarigamChemicals and other industrial manufacturingCommon effluent treatment, pollution prevention and hazardous-waste management
MorbiCeramics and associated manufacturingEnergy efficiency, suitable material recovery and waste reduction
Jamnagar and the coastal industrial beltPetroleum refining, petrochemicals and associated activitiesEnergy conservation, water efficiency and recovery of suitable industrial by-products

Industrial symbiosis

Industrial symbiosis occurs when separate enterprises cooperate so that a useful output, surplus resource or properly recovered by-product from one activity becomes an input for another.

For example, a manufacturing unit may generate clean, segregated metal scrap. Another enterprise may be able to process that scrap as a secondary raw material, reducing its requirement for newly extracted metal. In another case, usable surplus heat from an industrial process may support a nearby industrial activity if suitable infrastructure and safety conditions exist.

The main condition is compatibility. A substance must be suitable for its proposed use and must meet applicable environmental and safety requirements. A hazardous by-product cannot automatically be transferred to another factory simply because it has potential economic value.

Shared infrastructure and GIDC

The Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation (GIDC) develops industrial estates and related infrastructure. Depending on the estate and its requirements, facilities may include roads, water supply, drainage, power infrastructure and common effluent treatment arrangements.

Shared infrastructure is especially useful where individual small and medium enterprises may find specialised facilities expensive to establish independently. Nevertheless, each participating unit remains responsible for managing its wastes and effluents according to the conditions applicable to it.

The Gujarat Cleaner Production Centre (GCPC) promotes cleaner production through awareness programmes, assessments and demonstration projects. Cleaner production aims to reduce waste and pollution before they are generated, rather than relying only on treatment at the end of a process.

Industrial concentration is not the same as circularity

A cluster may contain many factories without any organised system for exchanging resources. Conversely, successful resource sharing requires more than proximity: it needs suitable material quality, reliable supply, infrastructure, coordination and compliance with regulations.

Industrial cluster: Industries located close together.
Industrial symbiosis: Industries cooperating through useful exchanges of compatible resources or by-products.
Common treatment: Several enterprises using a shared facility to manage specified wastes or effluents.

Prelims focus

  • The Ahmedabad–Vadodara belt is an important industrial concentration in Gujarat.
  • Morbi is associated with the ceramics industry.
  • GIDC develops industrial estates and supporting infrastructure.
  • GCPC promotes cleaner production and resource-efficient practices.
  • Trap: A common effluent treatment facility does not, by itself, establish that treated water is being reused.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 8, Resources and Development, chapter 5, Industries, printed pp. 50–53; NCERT, Class 12, India: People and Economy, chapter 8, Manufacturing Industries, printed pp. 91–96; Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation, Plug and Play facilities in GIDC, infrastructure section, consulted 2 November 2026; Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, Gujarat RAMP State Implementation Plan, industrial-cluster table for Morbi; Gujarat Cleaner Production Centre, Objectives, consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Nearby enterprises share infrastructure; symbiosis links segregated metal scrap to a compatible input, with environmental, safety and hazardous-material controls.
pictures.caption: Industrial symbiosis connects compatible resource outputs and inputs between enterprises.

title: Industrial Clusters and Opportunities for Resource Sharing

body:
Why wastewater reuse is important

Freshwater availability is uneven across Gujarat. Industrial demand, urban population growth and agricultural requirements increase pressure on available supplies. If usable wastewater is treated and reused, some demand for fresh water can be replaced without reducing the useful activity for which water is required.

Treated wastewater reuse means using wastewater again after treatment has made it suitable for an identified purpose. It is particularly valuable when the intended use does not require drinking-water quality.

The principle is known as fit-for-purpose water use: water quality should be appropriate for the particular activity and should comply with the standards that apply to that use.

From municipal sewage to reusable water

Municipal wastewater is collected through a sewerage network and conveyed to a sewage treatment plant (STP). Treatment removes pollutants to the degree required for the intended discharge or reuse.

Where a higher quality is needed, additional or tertiary treatment may be provided. This can make treated water suitable for particular industrial or other non-potable applications, subject to the required standards and safeguards.

Potential usePurposeImportant condition
Industrial coolingReduce dependence on fresh industrial water suppliesWater quality must meet the cooling system's requirements
Selected industrial processesReplace freshwater inputs where technically suitableProduct and process quality must not be compromised
Gardening and landscapingReduce use of potable-quality water for plantsHealth, soil and water-quality safeguards must be followed
Construction activitiesUse suitably treated water for permitted construction purposesRelevant quality and use requirements must be met
Lake restoration or other urban usesSupport planned non-potable applicationsEcological quality and public-health safeguards are essential

Reclaimed water should not be assumed safe for drinking. Potable use requires a substantially different assessment and the applicable drinking-water safeguards. Similarly, using untreated industrial effluent for irrigation is not equivalent to safe wastewater reuse.

Gujarat's Policy for Reuse of Treated Waste Water

The Government of Gujarat launched its Policy for Reuse of Treated Waste Water on 28 May 2018. Its objectives include increasing sewage collection, treating collected wastewater, promoting reuse and reducing dependence on freshwater resources.

Among the policy's stated objectives were reusing 70% of treated wastewater by 2025 and 100% by 2030. These percentages are policy targets. They must not be interpreted as verified achievements.

Status at the content cutoff of 2 November 2026: The 2025 target date has passed, while the 2030 target date is still in the future. The cited policy documents establish the targets but do not establish that Gujarat achieved the 70% target in 2025. A target and a measured result are different facts.

Surat: an important Gujarat example

Surat provides a documented example of municipal wastewater being converted into a useful industrial resource. The Surat Municipal Corporation's 2019 action plan reported that a 40 million litres per day (MLD) net-output tertiary treatment facility at Bamroli had been supplying industrial-grade treated water to the Pandesara GIDC industrial area since 2014.

The facility used additional treatment to produce water suitable for industrial customers. By replacing part of the industrial demand for conventional freshwater supplies, the project demonstrated a practical connection between municipal wastewater management and industrial resource efficiency.

A Press Information Bureau release dated 24 September 2024 separately reported that Surat had established 4 tertiary treatment plants with a combined installed capacity of 116 MLD. The 40 MLD figure describes the Bamroli facility in the 2019 action plan, whereas 116 MLD describes the combined capacity reported in 2024. They are different measures from different dated reports and should not be added together.

Benefits and limitations

Wastewater reuse can reduce freshwater withdrawals, create a dependable source for suitable industrial needs and reduce the quantity of treated effluent requiring discharge. However, these benefits depend on effective treatment, suitable distribution infrastructure and continuing compliance with water-quality requirements.

Collection and treatment are separate from reuse. A city may treat a large volume of sewage but reuse only a small portion. Likewise, a treatment plant's installed capacity does not necessarily equal the volume of treated water actually reused.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarat launched its treated-wastewater reuse policy on 28 May 2018.
  • The policy stated reuse targets of 70% by 2025 and 100% by 2030.
  • Surat's Bamroli project supplies treated water to the Pandesara industrial area.
  • Surat's 2019 action plan recorded a 40 MLD net-output tertiary treatment facility at Bamroli.
  • A government release dated 24 September 2024 reported 4 tertiary treatment plants in Surat with a combined installed capacity of 116 MLD.
  • Trap: A policy target, treatment capacity and actual quantity reused are not interchangeable.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, India: People and Economy, chapter 6, Water Resources, section Recycle and Reuse of Water, printed p. 67; Surat Municipal Corporation, Action Plan: Reuse and Recycle of Treated Wastewater, 2019, pp. 4–6, including policy objectives and Bamroli facility; Gujarat Water Supply and Sewerage Board, Revised Action Plan for Reuse of Treated Waste Water in the State of Gujarat, Policy and Vision sections, reproduced in Gujarat Pollution Control Board's report submitted to the National Green Tribunal on 24 August 2021; Press Information Bureau, Surat Municipal Corporation wastewater-reuse release, 24 September 2024. Sources consulted 2 November 2026.]
